item.title: 6. Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors
item.description:
Body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs) â€” including hair-pulling (trichotillomania), skin-picking (excoriation disorder), and nail-biting â€” are surprisingly common, affecting an estimated 2â€“5% of the population. Despite their prevalence, BFRBs are among the least well-monitored conditions in behavioral health. The primary reason is measurement: BFRBs are episodic, often automatic, and frequently occur outside of clinical settings. Self-report is unreliable (many patients are unaware of their behaviors in real time), and observational assessment is impractical for continuous monitoring. The result is that clinicians have almost no objective data on when, where, and how often these behaviors occur in daily life.

Wearable sensor technologies offer a potential solution. Modern wristbands and smartwatches contain accelerometers, gyroscopes, and physiological sensors (heart rate, electrodermal activity) that can capture the hand movements and autonomic signatures associated with BFRBs. The challenge is computational: extracting a reliable behavioral signal from noisy, multimodal sensor data in uncontrolled environments, where the target behaviors must be distinguished from the thousands of ordinary hand movements a person makes each day.

This project develops methods for automated BFRB detection using multimodal sensor fusion from wearable devices. The approach combines accelerometer, gyroscope, and physiological signals using multimodal learning techniques to identify BFRB episodes in naturalistic settings.

The manuscript is in preparation for IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics.
